html:
SMTO-GML-0035 — This sign-in link has expired or was already used

GUID: e82fb77c-0a2d-4d3c-881d-611c85fe1ea3
Slug: oauth-callback-state-invalid
Domain: GML · Subsystem: gml

What happened

  • Your browser came back to SMTO from a sign-in page that is too old, was already finished once, or doesn't belong to the current request. SMTO ignored it, so nothing was connected by it.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Close this browser tab and return to the SMTO conversation where the Task asked you to sign in. This page came from an old or already used sign-in, so it can't be used again.
  2. If the Task still shows 'Complete OAuth authorization to continue', select Open authorization page and finish signing in within a few minutes, in that one tab. Each sign-in link works only once and only for a short time, usually about ten minutes.
  3. If there's no sign-in prompt anymore, ask SMTO again in the conversation so it shows a new Open authorization page link. A new request creates a fresh sign-in that hasn't expired.
  4. Don't copy sign-in addresses, codes or passwords into the conversation. Sign-in codes are private, and SMTO only accepts them through the browser sign-in.

What success looks like

  • The browser shows 'Authorization received. You can close this window and return to the application.' and the Task continues.

If it still fails

  • If every new link also fails, select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO; the return address registered for that service may not match this SMTO server. Don't share codes or tokens in the conversation or in screenshots.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • The HTTP-connection OAuth callback (/api/agent/http/oauth/callback) did not match an unexpired, unused state with the same redirect URI, or arrived without a valid authorization code, so it returned 400.

What this means

  • Run-owned HTTP OAuth callback cannot match an unconsumed unexpired state with the exact redirect, or an accepted callback lacks a bounded nonempty code. Gmail provider receipts and exact account/message identities determine effects. Authorization, pagination or presentation failure cannot undo a send or other mutation; diagnostic rendering performs no mailbox or OAuth request.

Why this can happen

  • Run-owned HTTP OAuth callback cannot match an unconsumed unexpired state with the exact redirect, or an accepted callback lacks a bounded nonempty code.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect the original owning connection/state and redirect; this shared callback is not limited to Gmail.

How to fix it

  • Each OAuth state is single-use, expires after its provider-given lifetime (default 10 minutes, at most 30) and is lost on Server restart, and the callback URL must exactly match the redirect URI used to start it. Start a fresh authorization from the waiting Task's prompt and complete it once in one tab; confirm the OAuth client's registered redirect URI matches the scheme, host, port and path the Server receives. Never put codes or tokens in prompts.
  • Start a fresh authorization through the owning connection’s OAuth flow and complete that one flow. Do not reuse callback URLs or paste tokens into prompts.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • The supported owning OAuth flow completes once with matching state and redirect.

What not to do

  • Do not put credentials in task text, command arguments, screenshots or diagnostic reports.

Technical notes

  • Gmail provider receipts and exact account/message identities determine effects. Authorization, pagination or presentation failure cannot undo a send or other mutation; diagnostic rendering performs no mailbox or OAuth request.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
